result: Zebrafish neuromasts consist of three cell classes (hair cells, sustentacular cells, and mantle cells) organized in radial symmetry with a planar polarity axis. The organ contains approximately 60-70 cells with consistent proportions: ~40 sustentacular cells, 8-10 mantle cells, and 14-16 hair cells. Non-sensory cells can proliferate while hair cells are postmitotic.
evaluation: These claims describe the baseline neuromast architecture and are well-supported by direct observations, transgenic marker expression patterns (Figure 1), quantitative cell counts, and citations to established literature. The structural organization is clearly demonstrated through multiple imaging modalities.

result: Laser ablation provides precise cell elimination without collateral damage. Complete neuromast ablation is irreversible in larval zebrafish, with interneuromast cells not proliferating after complete organ removal.
evaluation: The laser ablation method is validated through time-lapse imaging (Figure 1M-P, Video 1) showing targeted cell removal. Complete ablation irreversibility is demonstrated with adequate sample sizes (n=22 and n=9) over 7 days (Figure 2). BrdU labeling confirms lack of interneuromast cell proliferation.

result: Neuromasts exhibit isotropic regenerative capacity, regenerating to ~70% of normal cell number by 7 days post-injury regardless of which half is ablated (posterior, dorsal, or mantle cells). Interneuromast cells are not essential for regeneration, though they may contribute. Sustentacular cells are tri-potent progenitors capable of self-renewal and generating both mantle and hair cells.
evaluation: This major finding is supported by systematic ablation experiments with appropriate sample sizes (n=5-15) across multiple conditions (Figure 3). The isotropic capacity is demonstrated by identical outcomes from different ablation patterns. The tri-potency of sustentacular cells is logically inferred from the observation that they can regenerate all cell types when mantle cells are completely removed.

result: Neuromasts reduced to 4-10 cells (>95% loss) can regenerate to recover ~70% of normal cell count with proper radial symmetry, cell-class composition, apicobasal polarity, and planar polarity by 7 days post-injury. Regeneration proceeds through wound closure (0-24 hpi), rapid cell proliferation and proportion restoration (1-3 dpi), and slower growth (3-7 dpi). As few as four supporting cells can initiate integral organ regeneration.
evaluation: This remarkable finding is well-documented through extensive time-lapse imaging (n=15), quantitative analysis of cell numbers and proportions (Figure 4K-M), and verification of all polarity axes (Figure 4Q-W). The recovery of planar polarity even without interneuromast cells (n=16) strengthens the conclusion of autonomous regenerative capacity.

result: Sustentacular and mantle founder cells exhibit distinct proliferative behaviors during regeneration. Sustentacular cells undergo 3-5 divisions (averaging 19±6 hr to first division) and produce all three cell classes through predominantly symmetric divisions (97%): 78% SS, 16% HH, 3% MM, and 3% asymmetric SM. Mantle cells divide less frequently (27±5 hr to division, with 14/30 not dividing) and produce only mantle cells through symmetric divisions.
evaluation: These quantitative findings are based on comprehensive cell tracking of 106 founder cells (76 sustentacular, 30 mantle) across 15 time-lapse recordings totaling 763 tracks and >100,000 spatiotemporal coordinates (Figure 5). The statistical measures are clearly reported with appropriate sample sizes. The division patterns are directly observed and categorized systematically.

result: Neuromast regeneration is initially isotropic (0-60 hpi) with even distribution of cell divisions, then becomes territorialized with 74% of divisions occurring in polar regions after 60 hpi. Clones remain largely ipsilateral to founder cells (60-74% on same side), indicating that territorialization occurs through location-adaptive cellular differentiation rather than cell migration.
evaluation: The spatial analysis is well-supported by quantitative tracking data showing division locations across neuromast quadrants (Figure 6A-H). The ipsilateral retention of progeny is demonstrated with clear percentages from tracked clones. The conclusion about location-adaptive differentiation is a reasonable inference from the limited cell migration observed.

result: Sustentacular founder cells produce four clone types with varying frequencies: SH (sustentacular + hair, 37/72), S (sustentacular only, 21/72), SM (sustentacular + mantle, 12/72), and SHM (all three classes, 2/72). Mantle founder cells produce only M (mantle only) clones.
evaluation: Clone composition is directly observed and quantified from 72 sustentacular founder cell clones across 15 regenerating neuromasts (Figure 6I-K). The frequencies are clearly reported and the classification is based on direct observation of cell fates in tracked lineages.

result: Cell divisions occur in three coordinated waves peaking at 20, 28, and 38 hours post-injury, spaced 8-10 hours apart. Cell-cycle length is initially ~11±3 hr and increases slowly until 47 hpi, then increases more rapidly and variably. Above 24 cells, cycle lengths show large variation. Cell-cycle length and proliferative potential do not explain clone composition differences.
evaluation: The temporal dynamics are quantified from extensive tracking data with clear statistical measures (Figure 7A-G). The two-segment regression model provides objective identification of transition points. The lack of correlation between proliferation kinetics and clone type is demonstrated through direct comparison, though the statistical test used is not specified.

result: Machine learning analysis using random forest algorithm (83.1% accuracy) identifies mediolateral position as the best predictor of cell fate. SH vs SM clones can be predicted with high accuracy (MCC=0.63±0.09), with distance to center and distance to mantle cells as most informative features. HH vs SM/MM divisions are highly predictable (MCC=0.91±0.07). SM/MM divisions occur at the periphery (never in anterior region), HH divisions near center, and SS divisions in between, suggesting spatially regulated differentiation to restore cell-class proportions.
evaluation: The machine learning approach is rigorous with proper cross-validation (leave-one-out on 15 samples), appropriate performance metrics (MCC to handle class imbalance), and comparison of 20 algorithms (Figure 8—supplement 1). The spatial patterns of division types are clearly demonstrated (Figure 8F). The conclusion about spatially regulated differentiation is well-supported by the predictive power of positional features.

result: Neuromast regeneration follows a hierarchical process: (1) founder cells reconstitute epithelium, (2) sustentacular cells proliferate to restore size, (3) daughter cells differentiate position-appropriately to recreate proportions and geometry, (4) epithelium returns to homeostatic low mitotic state. Cellular intercalation is rare. Neuromasts lack specialized repair cells; instead, progenitor behavior is a facultative status any sustentacular cell can acquire. No regenerative overshoot occurs.
evaluation: This synthesis of the regeneration process is well-supported by the comprehensive time-lapse data, lineage tracing, and quantitative analysis presented throughout the manuscript. The hierarchical stages are clearly demonstrated in the temporal progression data. The lack of specialized repair cells is a reasonable inference from the observation that any sustentacular cell can act as progenitor. The absence of overshoot is documented in the cell count data.

result: A mechanism exists that senses total cell number and cell-class balance during repair, possibly based on interplay between Fgf, Notch, and Wnt signaling pathways.
evaluation: While the accurate restoration of cell-class proportions without overshoot suggests such a sensing mechanism exists, this claim is speculative. The manuscript does not directly test signaling pathways or provide mechanistic evidence. The suggestion about Fgf/Notch/Wnt is based on integration with prior literature rather than experimental data from this study.

result: Machine learning and quantitative videomicroscopy reveal clear differences between sustentacular and mantle cells but do not indicate heterogeneity within the sustentacular-cell population.
evaluation: The distinct behaviors of sustentacular vs mantle cells are clearly demonstrated through lineage tracing and division analysis. The lack of detectable heterogeneity within sustentacular cells is supported by the inability to predict S vs SH or SM clones (low MCC values in Figure 8B), though this is essentially a negative result that doesn't rule out subtle heterogeneity below detection limits.

result: Previous studies show mantle cells can proliferate after tail-fin amputation to generate new neuromasts, up-regulate gene expression after injury, and constitute a quiescent pool re-entering cell cycle upon severe sustentacular cell depletion. They may form a stem-cell niche and could drive regeneration if all other cell classes are lost.
evaluation: These claims accurately summarize prior published work (properly cited). However, the speculation about mantle cells driving complete regeneration if all other cells are lost is not directly tested in this study or the cited work.

result: The authors propose a model where radial symmetry serves as a rheostat to identify damage sites and guide regeneration spatially through a polarized intact-injured axis. However, partial radial symmetry maintenance is not essential for regeneration, as neuromasts can regenerate from 4 cells. Partial structural maintenance and polarized responses may optimize repair by preventing superfluous production in undamaged areas.
evaluation: This is a proposed model (Figure 9) rather than a directly tested result. While the observation that 4 cells can regenerate a complete neuromast supports the conclusion that radial symmetry maintenance is not essential, the proposed rheostat mechanism and polarized axis are speculative interpretations not directly validated by experimental manipulation.

result: As few as four founder cells can re-organize local coherent planar polarity during repair. Based on prior work on Emx2 (which shows variegated expression in hair cells and controls their orientation), the authors suggest founder cells autonomously organize Emx2 expression during regeneration. Local coherent polarity appears self-organizing while global orientation may be controlled externally. Polarization occurs independently of innervation.
evaluation: The observation that 4-10 cells can regenerate proper planar polarity is well-documented (C38, n=10). However, the mechanistic explanation involving Emx2 is speculative, based on integration with cited work rather than direct testing in this study. The distinction between local self-organization and external global control is a reasonable interpretation but not definitively proven. The independence from innervation is from cited prior work.

result: Intact resident cells can rapidly recreate their microenvironment to rebuild neuromasts with normal organization from ~5% original size. While extracellular matrix could serve as a blueprint, cell-fate acquisition must be tissue-size dependent since geometric order is regained at <60% cellular content. Self-organization is proposed as the optimal morphogenetic process for repair because it requires minimal prior information and is robust to signal failures.
evaluation: The observation that neuromasts regain geometric order at <60% size (2 dpi) is well-documented. However, the claims about self-organization vs. self-assembly are interpretive. The manuscript does not definitively rule out extracellular matrix guidance or other external cues. The argument for self-organization as optimal is theoretical rather than experimentally demonstrated.
